analysis.one_liner: Requires warrants before officials search Americans' communications collected under foreign surveillance program.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate Intelligence Committee the day it was introduced and never moved, leaving it with no cosponsors and no vote as Section 702 neared its June 12, 2026 expiration.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act so that government officials cannot search the communications of Americans without a warrant, the person's consent, a true emergency, or a narrow cybersecurity need. Every search would have to be documented in a record system that names the officer and the reason. At the same time, the bill would extend the underlying surveillance program itself by nine months, to March 12, 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans whose emails, texts, and calls are held by phone and internet companies. Under current law, the FBI and intelligence agencies can search that raw data for information about Americans without a warrant; the bill would require a court order, consent, or a documented emergency before anyone could read what turns up, and would create an audit trail for every search [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose communications pass through US providers

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars federal officers from accessing the communications and sensitive information of US persons and people located in the US that is returned by a query of foreign-surveillance data, unless one of four narrow exceptions applies: an existing court order or warrant, a life-or-death emergency, the person's consent, or a defensive cybersecurity need [S2].
It also blocks queries that are not tied to a genuine foreign-intelligence purpose, closing the loophole that lets officials search Americans' data for ordinary investigative reasons [S2].

Every query and every access to results would have to be logged with the search terms, the date, the officer's identity, and the justification, and agency heads would have to report on compliance to Congress and the courts — creating the first real audit trail for these searches [S2].

If an official invokes the emergency exception improperly, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court would review it within 7 days and any improperly obtained information would be barred from use in court or other proceedings [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The FBI, CIA, and NSA would lose their current ability to search collected communications for Americans' information without a warrant, and would bear the cost of building and maintaining the required query record system. Telecommunications and internet providers would remain legally compelled to assist the government's collection under the extended program [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill extends Section 702 itself to March 12, 2027, keeping alive a program that sweeps up large volumes of foreigners' communications — and Americans' communications that touch them — rather than letting it expire on June 12, 2026 [S2].

The emergency and defensive-cybersecurity exceptions allow warrantless access with only after-the-fact reporting to courts and Congress within 7 days, and the cybersecurity exception's scope is defined by the agencies themselves [S2].

Critics of Section 702 would note that the bill treats a sunset of the program as a problem to be deferred rather than a decision, while defenders of the program argue the warrant requirement would slow urgent counterintelligence and cyber investigations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The warrant requirement is a real, substantive protection for Americans' private communications, and the documentation mandate would create accountability that does not exist today. But the price is a nine-month extension of the bulk collection program itself, and the emergency and cybersecurity carve-outs leave meaningful room for warrantless access. It is a compromise bill: a genuine gain for privacy that also keeps the surveillance architecture running.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Intelligence Committee on the day it was introduced and has sat there without a hearing, cosponsor, or vote; Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on June 10, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Select Committee on Intelligence, which has taken no further action on it [S4].
No senator has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

The bill arrives just before Section 702's June 12, 2026 expiration date, which it would push to March 12, 2027; its effective-date provision is drafted so the extension applies from enactment or June 11, 2026, whichever is earlier [S2].
The warrantless-query prohibition, exceptions, and query record system would all be written directly into Section 702(f) of FISA [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the intelligence agencies are better off: they continue operating under existing rules, with no warrant requirement enacted, and the question of Section 702's future remains open in committee rather than on the floor.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and has scheduled no hearing or markup.

against.name: FBI and intelligence community leadership
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed warrant requirements for 702 queries of Americans' communications, arguing they would hinder urgent investigations.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no votes, so no partisan pattern has emerged.

industries.note: The agencies gain nine more months of Section 702 collection authority, but lose the power to search the collected data for Americans' information without a warrant and must build an audit system. Their institutional interest in unrestricted access runs against the privacy interest of ordinary people, though the bill does not shut them down.

Section 702 legally compels electronic communication service providers to help the government collect communications; extending the program entrenches their role as the collection pipeline. The bill imposes no new obligations on them beyond the status quo.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Intelligence Committee with zero cosponsors, and Section 702's expiration date falls days after introduction. Standalone reform bills at this stage are typically superseded by a leadership-negotiated reauthorization or short-term extension; unless Wyden can attach the warrant requirement to a larger FISA bill, it is likely to die in committee at the end of this Congress.
